Χρῶνται δὲ τῷ ῥητῷ τούτῳ καὶ οἱ ἀπὸ Μαρκίωνος, καὶ ἀναισθήτως κωλύουσι τὸν
γάμον, λέγοντες τὴν ἁγνείαν πρόσταγμα εἶναι τοῦ ἄλλου θεοῦ ὃν ἀνέ πλασαν παρὰ
τὸν δημιουργόν. πλὴν ἐκ τοῦ ῥητοῦ ἔστιν αὐτοὺς συμβιβάσαι ὅτι κακῶς κωλύουσι
τὸν γάμον, κακῶς καὶ διαιροῦσι τὴν θεότητα. εἰ γὰρ χάρισμά ἐστι τῷ μὲν οὕτως τῷ
δὲ οὕτως, χάρισμά ἐστι καὶ ὁ γάμος· εἰ χάρισμα καὶ ὁ γάμος, κακῶς κωλύεται τὸ
χάρισμα ὁ γάμος· εἰ ὁ μὲν οὕτως ὁ δὲ οὕτως ἀπὸ θεοῦ, δῆλον ὅτι εἷς θεὸς ὁ δεδωκὼς
τὴν ἁγνείαν καὶ ὁ δεδωκὼς τὸν γάμον, καὶ εἷς ὁ τοῦ νόμου καὶ τοῦ εὐαγγελίου θεός
ἐστιν, ὃν κατήγγειλαν πρότερον μὲν οἱ προφῆται ὕστερον δὲ Χριστὸς Ἰησοῦς. 35 vii
8–12 [Λέγω δὲ τοῖς ἀγάμοις καὶ ταῖς χήραις, καλὸν αὐτοῖς ἐὰν μείνωσιν ὡς κἀγώ· εἰ
δὲ οὐκ ἐγκρατεύονται, γαμησάτωσαν· κρεῖττον γάρ ἐστι γαμῆσαι ἢ πυροῦσθαι. τοῖς
δὲ γεγαμηκόσι παραγγέλλω, οὐκ ἐγὼ ἀλλ' ὁ κύριος, γυναῖκα ἀπὸ ἀνδρὸς μὴ
χωρισθῆναι–ἐὰν δὲ καὶ χωρισθῇ, μενέτω ἄγαμος ἢ τῷ ἀνδρὶ καταλλαγήτω–καὶ
ἄνδρα γυναῖκα μὴ ἀφιέναι. τοῖς δὲ λοιποῖς λέγω ἐγώ, οὐχ ὁ κύριος.] [Ὠριγένους]
Τινὲς τῶν καθ' ἡμᾶς ὑπὲρ ἃ γέγραπται διδάσκουσι· καὶ οἰόμενοί τι ποιεῖν, δέον
προτρέπειν ἐπὶ μονογαμίαν μετὰ τοῦ μὴ βρόχον ἐπιτιθέναι τοῖς μὴ δυναμένοις,
τοῦτο μὲν οὐ ποιοῦσιν, ἀνάγκην δὲ ἐπιτιθέασι καὶ θέλουσι μὴ συνάγειν τοὺς
διγάμους μηδὲ κοινωνεῖν αὐτοῖς ὡς παραβεβηκόσιν, οὐκ αἰ δούμενοι οὐδὲ τὰς τοῦ
ἀποστόλου φωνάς. ὁ γὰρ λέγων τοῖς ἀγάμοις καὶ ταῖς χήραις, εἰ οὐκ ἐγκρατεύονται
γαμησάτωσαν, ἄντικρυς ἐπέτρεψεν μετὰ τὸν πρῶτον γάμον μετὰ τὸ χηρεῦσαι
γυναῖκα γαμῆσαι, μετὰ τοῦ λοιδορῆσαι τὸν γαμοῦντα, μετὰ τοῦ λοιδορῆσαι τὴν
γαμουμένην· εἶπεν γὰρ Εἰ οὐκ ἐγκρατεύονται, γαμησάτωσαν· ὅρα γὰρ εἰ μὴ ἤδη
κατηγορία ἐστὶ τὸ μὴ ἐγκρατεύεσθαι, οἷον ἔστι λέγεσθαι ἀνθρώποις χριστιανοῖς
Κάλλιον γαμῆσαι ἢ πυροῦσθαι, πύρωσιν ὀνομάσαντος αὐτοῦ τὴν ἐπιθυμίαν τῆ
αρκὸ μὴ σβεννυ μένην ὑπὸ τοῦ λόγου ἀλλὰ κρατοῦσαν τῆς ψυχῆς τοῦ ἁμαρτωλοῦ.
Ἡμεῖς οὖν διδαχθέντες ὑπὸ τοῦ ἀποστόλου οὐ κωλύομεν τὴν διγαμίαν, συγκρίσει
γὰρ πυρώσεως αἱρετωτέρα διγαμία· ὅταν δὲ κακοῖς συγκρινόμενον κρεῖττον εἶναί
pass_a_gloss: Marcionites seize this verse and ban marriage without sense, claiming chastity is a precept of another deity they invent beside the Maker. From the verse itself one can show their ban is wrong and their split of deity is wrong. If gift comes to one person one way and to another another way, marriage too is gift; if marriage is gift, forbidding that gift is wrong; if both modes come from God, one God grants chastity and marriage, and one God stands behind law and gospel—the one prophets first announced and Christ Jesus later. I speak to the unmarried and widows: remaining as I remain is fine for them; yet if they lack continence they should marry, since marrying beats burning. To those already married I give charge—the Lord, not I—that a wife must not leave her husband (and if she leaves she must stay single or return to him) and that a husband must not dismiss his wife. To everyone else I speak, I not the Lord. Certain teachers among us go past Scripture; thinking they achieve something, though they should urge one marriage without trapping those who cannot keep it, they instead force necessity and refuse to gather or share with the twice married as if they had broken faith, ignoring even Paul. The voice that tells unmarried people and widows to marry when they lack continence plainly allows a widow a later marriage—while still blaming the one who marries. Saying “if they lack continence, marry” already charges the lack; telling Christians “marrying beats burning” names burning as fleshly desire the Word has not quenched, ruling the sinner’s soul. Taught by Paul we do not ban remarriage; next to burning it is preferable. Yet what looks better only beside evils is not itself good. A second marriage is not temperance and does not match Adam the first formed; one cannot tell a second wife “this is bone from my bones and flesh from my flesh.” Abraham knew Hagar and later Keturah, yet at death only Sarah the natural wife lay with him in the tomb. Jacob knew Rachel, Leah, and the maidservants, yet only Leah shared his tomb. That belongs to the fathers’ mystical arrangement; the man who takes a second wife today does not claim he is finishing a mystery. Paul will ask those reading the law whether they hear it: a certain man had two sons, and the rest; over him one will not also hear “these things are allegorized, for these women are two covenants,” for those events happened as types for them and were written for us on whom the ages’ ends have arrived. I tell widows and the unmarried that remaining as I remain is fine. That is a second good; a prior good is not touching a woman. What is the second? Remaining as I remain; yet if they lack continence they should marry, since marrying beats burning. So those in a first marriage who have never faced a second should train in chastity, so that if something human occurs they are not caught unpracticed and act shamefully. Preferable then is a second marriage—he is not speaking of a first here, as “to burn” makes plain. From here he shifts to another statute: to the married I give charge, the Lord not I; that statute toward the married is the Lord’s, not mine. He also keeps a needed note: “married” names both when husband and wife believe. That he left unequally yoked people out of “married” is clear when he adds: to the rest I speak, I not the Lord. pass_b_english: Those from Marcion also use this saying, and without sense they forbid marriage, saying that chastity is a command of the other god whom they invented beside the Creator. Yet from the saying itself one can prove to them that they forbid marriage badly, and badly divide the Godhead. For if there is a gift to one in this way and to another in that, marriage also is a gift; if marriage is a gift, marriage the gift is badly forbidden; if the one in this way and the other in that are from God, it is clear that one God is the giver of chastity and the giver of marriage, and one is the God of the law and of the gospel, whom the prophets first proclaimed and later Christ Jesus.

But I say to the unmarried and to the widows that it is good for them if they remain as I also am; but if they are not practicing self-control, let them marry, for it is better to marry than to burn. To the married I give charge—not I but the Lord—that a wife not be separated from a husband—but if she is separated, let her remain unmarried or be reconciled to the husband—and that a husband not send away a wife. To the rest I say, I not the Lord (1 Corinthians 7:8–12).

Some among us teach beyond what is written; and thinking they are doing something, when they ought to exhort to single marriage without laying a snare on those who cannot, they do not do this, but impose necessity and wish not to gather the twice-married nor to share with them as with those who have transgressed, not respecting even the apostle’s voices. For the one who says to the unmarried and the widows, if they are not continent let them marry, openly permitted after the first marriage, after a woman has been widowed, to marry—while blaming the one who marries and the one who is married; for he said: If they are not continent, let them marry. See whether not being continent is not already an accusation—as when it is said to Christian people: Better to marry than to burn—he naming as burning the desire of the flesh not quenched by the Word but mastering the sinner’s soul. We therefore, taught by the apostle, do not forbid remarriage; for by comparison with burning, remarriage is more choiceworthy. Yet when something is thought better by comparison with evils, that thing is clearly not good. The second marriage is not temperance; it is not according to the nature of Adam the first-formed; for one cannot say to the second wife: This now is bone of my bones and flesh of my flesh (Genesis 2:23). Abraham had also Hagar, and came to be also with Keturah; yet when he died, none was laid with him except the wife by nature; for Abraham and Sarah were in the tomb. And Jacob too, even if he had been with Rachel and with Leah and also with the maidservants, yet in the tomb only Leah was with him. With the mystical economy of the fathers; yet surely even now the one who takes a second does not say: I am fulfilling a mystical economy. For Paul will come saying: Tell me, you who read the law, do you not hear the law? For it is written: So-and-so had two sons, and so on; it will not also be said over him: These things are allegorized, for these women are two covenants; for these things happened typically to them, but were written for us upon whom the ends of the ages have come (Galatians 4:21–24; 1 Corinthians 10:11).

I say to the widows and to the unmarried that it is good for them if they remain as I also am. This is a second good; for there is another good first before this: it is good for a man not to touch a woman. What second good? It is good for them if they remain as I also am; but if they are not continent, let them marry; for it is better to marry than to burn. Therefore those in first marriages who have not yet experienced second ones should practice chastity, that if something human happens they may not, caught untrained, behave shamefully. Better, then, to marry a second marriage—for he does not mean the first here, as is clear from the wording “to burn.” From here he passes to another legislation: To the married I give charge, not I but the Lord; the legislation toward the married is not from me but from the Lord. At the same time he keeps a necessary observation: he named “married” when both are believers, both the husband and the wife. That he did not name among the married the others who are unequally yoked is clear from his adding: To the rest I say, I not the Lord. Are the rest then not married?
